A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GRULSIF research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support a reliable comparison despite substantial changes in formulation and evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic and MNIST two-sample-testing experiments in Section 6 and Table 1, with additional alpha-sensitivity results in Appendix B.3 and Table 2.

after.justification: V2 reports original likelihood-ratio and divergence-estimation experiments across four synthetic scenarios, including convergence and sensitivity results in Figures 2–9.

M1.justification: V1 uses raw dictionary kernel evaluations and Euclidean coefficient penalties (Equations 3–7). V2 introduces Gram-matrix-weighted RKHS penalties and Nyström-normalized features, changing the estimator and its updates (Equations 18 and 36–39). The coherence-based dictionary strategy remains, but the two-sample permutation-test pipeline is removed.

E1.justification: The earlier Gaussian/uniform and bivariate-Gaussian scenarios are reworked as v2 Synth.Ia/Ib. V2 removes MNIST and the evaluated two-sample-testing application, focusing on direct likelihood-ratio estimation. It also adds Barabási–Albert ego-network scenarios, including a Gaussian-mixture setting.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates MMD median and MMD aggreg alongside POOL, RULSIF, ULSIF and KLIEP. V2 retains the latter four comparators but removes both MMD methods, eliminating the statistical-test comparator family from the evaluation (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 2 and Figures 2–5). POOL was already present in v1.

E3.justification: V1 evaluates permutation-based decisions using precision, recall and F1. V2 evaluates likelihood-ratio MSE using 10,000 independent held-out samples and reports divergence estimates. Plotted training sample sizes extend to 250 and 500, and the alpha sweep changes from {0, 0.1, 0.5} to {0.01, 0.1, 0.5}. V2's exact SBM size is unclear: Table 1 specifies 25 nodes per cluster, whereas Section 6.1 says 20.

E4.justification: The no-graph POOL comparison and alpha-sensitivity analysis already exist in v1, including Appendix B.3. V2 retains these principal ablation questions, reworks them around estimation convergence, and adds node-group diagnostics of divergence bias and dispersion in Figures 2–9.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly reports means and standard deviations over 50 generated instances, together with permutation-based significance levels. V2 presents convergence curves and node-group boxplots without specifying experiment repetition counts or comparable across-run uncertainty estimates. This substantially reduces explicit replication and uncertainty reporting; it does not establish that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: V1's synthetic and MNIST precision/recall/F1 results are replaced by likelihood-ratio MSE curves and divergence-estimation distributions in v2 Figures 2–9. New findings include POOL overtaking GRULSIF at n=500 in Figure 2 after GRULSIF leads at smaller sample sizes. These are results under revised tasks, estimators and settings, not same-setting performance gains between versions.

T1.justification: V2 adds vector-valued RKHS and representer-theorem derivations, explicit statistical assumptions, and excess-risk/L2 convergence bounds with extensive proofs in Appendix C. The CBCGD convergence analysis is revised for Gram-matrix penalties. V1's permutation-test validity theorem and its Appendix A.4 proof are removed.

C1.justification: The central collaborative LRE claim remains, but v2 makes statistical convergence guarantees, conditions favoring collaboration, and POOL's standalone value central contributions. V1 instead emphasizes its two-sample-testing application and superiority on synthetic and MNIST tests. Application development becomes future work in v2's conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 explains collaborative gains through sample size, graph size, smoothness and RKHS capacity, including regimes where collaboration offers little advantage. It acknowledges cross-node independence as a strong theoretical assumption and interprets POOL's gains through shared dictionaries, Nyström features and joint tuning. Alpha selection becomes an application-dependent tradeoff, extending v1's recommendation near 0.1.

D1.justification: V2 documents feature-statistic precomputation, Gram-matrix stabilization options and more detailed computational costs in Section 5 and Appendix A.3. Dictionary coherence thresholds and most cross-validation grids are retained. V1's explicit baseline-software links and permutation-test implementation details disappear.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around vector-valued kernels, learning theory and Nyström approximation, adding works such as Micchelli and Pontil, Bartlett et al., and Williams and Seeger. The previously cited Yousefi et al. becomes a central theoretical foundation. MMD and other testing-specific references are removed as the paper shifts toward general LRE and its potential applications.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten. Preliminaries are reorganized into dedicated conceptual subsections, convergence analysis receives a main section, and the alpha discussion moves from Appendix B.3 into Section 6.2. Appendices and reference placement are reorganized, beyond changes required by new scientific content alone.

P2.justification: V1's dense performance tables are replaced by scenario/comparator summary tables and extensive convergence-curve and boxplot grids. V2 also adds a graphical problem illustration, reformats pseudocode with line numbers, and adopts a different title-page and running-header layout. These substantially change how the method and evidence are presented.

improvement.justification: V2 improves methodological depth through an explicit RKHS/Nyström formulation, conditional error analysis in Section 4 and Appendix C, and direct estimation-error and bias diagnostics. However, it loses the MNIST/application validation and explicit 50-instance uncertainty reporting, while experimental descriptions contain conflicts with tables and figure axes. The theoretical and diagnostic gains support a net improvement, but these empirical-reporting weaknesses limit its overall extent.
